articles.title_orig: Trump Aides Seek to Jump Start Diplomacy With Iran as Crisis Widens
articles.title_zh: Trump Aides Seek to Jump Start Diplomacy With Iran as Crisis Widens
articles.content_orig:
FDD’s Behnam Ben Taleblu says Iran’s deeply buried nuclear-linked site poses a growing military challenge as Tehran hardens entrances and rebuilds sensitive facilities.
New satellite imagery shows Iran has added new defenses around tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried nuclear-linked site President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike, as Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution aimed at preserving international monitoring of sanctions on Tehran.
The Institute for Science and International Security said in a report released Thursday that satellite imagery from Sept. 11 shows earthen roadblocks remain in place on roads leading to Pickaxe Mountain’s western tunnel portals near the Natanz nuclear complex. The institute said the continued restricted access reinforces its assessment that the facility is not currently being used for normal operations, while assessing that valuable equipment or materials remain inside.
The report also identified additional soil placed over one western tunnel portal and over a nearby cluster of entrances first built in 2007. The institute said the added soil increases the amount of earth protecting the entrances and helps harden them against aerial bombardment.
EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE
An overview of Iran’s Natanz nuclear complex and nearby Pickaxe Mountain, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies.)
The findings come one week after Trump issued his latest warning over Pickaxe Mountain .
"We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe," Trump told reporters last week. "I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard."
Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of attacking the site. In a July 28 "Fox & Friends" interview highlighted by the White House , Trump said the U.S. was watching Pickaxe closely and knew "exactly what’s going on," adding that Washington could "take out Pickaxe" if diplomacy failed.
Pickaxe Mountain lies roughly two kilometers from Natanz and features multiple tunnel entrances leading into a deeply buried underground complex. Construction began in 2020 following sabotage that damaged an advanced centrifuge assembly facility at Natanz, and Iranian officials subsequently said a replacement underground facility was being built for advanced centrifuge production. Analysts estimate portions of the facility may be buried at least 100 meters beneath the mountain. Iran has said there is no nuclear activity at the site.
TRUMP SAYS US HAS 'MASSIVE' MUNITIONS STOCKPILE, VOWS 'TREASONOUS' LEAKERS BEING HUNTED DOWN
A closer view of tunnel entrances at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies)
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that some analysts believe the opportunity for a straightforward strike on Pickaxe Mountain may already have passed.
"The window to strike Pickaxe Mountain, according to some, has already expired because the regime has dug an underground nuclear facility several times deeper than Fordow," Ben Taleblu said. But he argued that Washington retains military options even if destroying the underground complex itself proves difficult.
"Washington can do what it’s traditionally been able to do with sites that are underground, hardened and fortified, and that’s to bury their entrances and raise the political cost to the Islamic Republic of being able to dig out," he said.
"While there may not be the perfect munition just yet, Uncle Sam always has a bigger bomb," Ben Taleblu added. "And in the meantime, what they can do is show that they mean business by burying the entrances."
NUCLEAR EXPERTS URGE TRUMP NOT TO LET IRAN STEER TALKS AWAY FROM REGIME'S ATOMIC THREAT
A satellite view shows an overview of the Natanz nuclear facility and Pickaxe Mountain, near Natanz, Iran, June 30, 2026 (Vantor/Handout via Reuters)
The Pickaxe findings came alongside signs of reconstruction at another sensitive Iranian facility .
In a separate report Thursday, the institute said Iran was "rapidly moving forward" with reconstruction of Taleghan 2 at the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran. Vantor Technologies satellite imagery from Sept. 13 shows Iran erected a tarp over the destroyed hardened facility, obscuring work underneath from satellite or aerial observation, while dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete equipment and cranes were active around the site.
The institute said Iran also built new concrete reinforcement that could provide additional protection against aerial attack. Taleghan 2 was struck by Israel in October 2024 and again in March 2026 after Iran had rebuilt and hardened the facility. The institute said significant questions remain about Tehran’s plans for the site.
The military developments unfolded alongside a separate confrontation over Iran at the United Nations .
CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN
Satellite imagery shows the underlying structure of the rebuilt Taleghan 2 facility at Iran’s Parchin military complex encased within a concrete "sarcophagus," prior to being covered with soil in Feb. 13, 2026. (Vantor Technologies with annotations by ISIS)
Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-authored Security Council resolution that would have extended for another year, until September 2027, the mandate of the Panel of Experts supporting the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee. The measure received 11 votes in favor, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.
The panel investigates alleged sanctions violations and reports on implementation. The dispute reflects a deeper split over whether UN sanctions suspended under the 2015 nuclear agreement were legally restored through the "snapback" mechanism. Most Council members maintain that the sanctions and related monitoring structures were revived, while Russia and China reject the legal and procedural validity of that position.
A day before the vote, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters in New York that Washington considers the sanctions legally restored .
"The snapback sanctions… occurred, the United States and this U.N. Security Council followed appropriate procedures for that to occur," Waltz said Wednesday at a news conference attended by Fox News Digital. "Those sanctions are in place and we expect those who are a party to fully enforce those sanctions."
Waltz said the expert panel is important because sanctioned companies and individuals can attempt to evade restrictions by changing names and corporate structures.
"The president has been clear, and the world community has been clear with resolution after resolution, that the Iranian regime cannot have a nuclear weapon," Waltz said.

Thursday also brought fresh U.N. scrutiny of both Washington and Tehran. An independent U.N. fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe two U.S. strikes on civilian sites in Iran in February constituted war crimes, while separately concluding that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on anti-government protests. The mission is investigative rather than judicial, and its findings do not themselves constitute criminal judgments.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Iran U.N. mission for comments but didn’t receive them in time for publication.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
articles.content_orig:
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu takes to his feet at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York later on Thursday, he does so at a critical point in both his political career and in his country’s long and fractious relationship with the international body.
Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide at the UN, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Those criticisms continue to shape the country’s fractious relationship with the body.
For Netanyahu, appearing in front of the UNGA for the 15th time, the stakes have rarely been higher. Addressing a domestic Israeli audience that polls show to be losing faith in him and his Likud party in the run-up to crucial elections later this year, Netanyahu has already pitched himself as Israel’s primary voice on the international stage.
Nevertheless, analysts say Netanyahu’s address could prove a pivotal moment domestically, amplified by international criticism of Israel and expected to dominate headlines and be carried live across the country’s television networks.
“This is a regular fixture for him,” former Israeli consul general in New York and ex-government adviser, Alon Pinkas, told Al Jazeera. “It’s his way of being seen in Israel as standing up against the world and of telling members that he will never give up or surrender. He’s also turned the event into some kind of national holiday in Israel, with everyone sitting down to watch the address on television. He’s brainwashed people in Israel into believing his speech is somehow an announcement of policy, stated in defiance of the [rest of the world] who don’t believe a word he says.”
Israeli leaders have long framed their stance towards the UN as one of defiance in the face of hostility. The UN has long been a platform for critics of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land and repeated attacks on its neighbours. It has included attempts to censure Israel over what UN investigators have described as apartheid in the West Bank, as well as accusations of genocide and pogroms across the occupied Palestinian territory since October 2023.
There have been numerous UNGA resolutions criticising Israel’s conduct – nearly all dismissed by Israeli lawmakers as evidence of institutional bias – culminating in Israel declaring UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres persona non grata and severely restricting the operations of the UN’s agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
“Generally speaking, many Israelis tend to see the UN as anti-Israeli,” Nimrod Goren, the president of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, Mitvim, said.
Against that background, criticism from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani – already cast as anti-Israel in the Israeli press – has drawn greater public attention to the event. Underscoring the sense of hostility towards Israel are stories within the country’s media suggesting that Netanyahu’s visit to New York has been curtailed due to unspecified security concerns, with the Israeli premier expected to fly out of New York on the same day as his arrival.
In response, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, who has repeatedly accused the organisation of waging “diplomatic terrorism” against the state, called for Mamdani’s arrest for what he said was the mayor’s incitement against New York’s Jewish community before Netanyahu’s visit.
“Netanyahu is going into his UNGA speech with not one but both eyes focused firmly on the upcoming Israeli election,” Goren said. “The speech is usually treated in Israel as a major event, receiving broad coverage and dominating the news cycle. Netanyahu will likely try to leverage this to bolster his image as a close ally of the US and to talk up the threat posed by Iran.”
Some have interpreted US President Donald Trump’s apparent lack of availability to meet Netanyahu during this trip as a sign of waning support. But US backing for Israel at the UN has remained steadfast since the October 7 attack and has contributed to growing frustration within the UN over what they see as Israel’s ability to resist international censure.
Alongside the creation of the Board of Peace, which shifted significant responsibility for Gaza’s future from the UN to the Trump-founded organisation, Washington has repeatedly used its veto at the UN Security Council (UNSC) to shield Israel from resolutions it opposes. The US has vetoed at least six UNSC resolutions on Gaza since October 2023, most of them demanding an immediate ceasefire.
“There seems to be genuine frustration within the UN General Assembly over the body’s failure to play a significant political role in Gaza and the West Bank, but also in its failure to protect its own staff and agencies,” Chatham House Associate Fellow Zizette Darkazally, who previously worked with the UN, said.
“However, it’s worth remembering the context the UN operates within in the occupied territories and the important humanitarian role it plays. The UN continues to get aid and medical support into Gaza and the West Bank, which are both areas where Israel has absolute control over access,” she said. “It’s also worth remembering that the UN is only as strong as the commitment of its member states.
“That, combined with a system of veto that’s more than 80 years old, has left the organisation weaker now than it had ever been,” she said of the confrontations between the UN and Israel. “And we’re seeing the effects of that, not just in Palestine, but in Yemen, Sudan and Iran, where the UN is playing next to no political role.”

articles.title_orig: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first
articles.title_zh: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first
articles.content_orig:
Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack
A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind in the world.
The agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time.
He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for taking "too long" to disclose the breach and said there would be "legal consequences".
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
Five days later, that government agency, Services Australia, escalated the email to Australia's cybersecurity centre before a government minister was notified and the prime minister alerted.
Albanese said he spoke to Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" as well as his "disappointment" that the company had taken months to reveal the breach and "the nature of the way" it did so.
The Australian leader said Altman had acknowledged there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
A "forensic investigation" led by the country's cybersecurity agency would aim to find out if other government systems were affected, Albanese said.
The probe would also assess if the matter needed to be dealt with by police, he said, noting there "will obviously be legal consequences".
Detailing the breach, Albanese said it had involved "public and non-public files" on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, home to "non-sensitive" data and statistics.
Three other government systems "may" also have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and two state-based agencies - the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health.
"No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing," Albanese said.
"Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable," he said.
Albanese said it took "too long" for OpenAI to inform Australian officials of the breach in June
OpenAI, in a statement, said it had "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation".
"In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," the statement said.
Albanese declined to answer whether he raised the matter with US President Donald Trump during their face-to-face meeting on Tuesday night in New York, where world leaders have gathered for the UN General Assembly.
Australia was one of 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for the development of AI.
Cybersecurity experts told the BBC the incident is a wake up call for regulators, given that AI agents are becoming more widely available for individual and commercial use.
Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of NSW Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC that though this is the first known incident where AI agents have chosen to breach a government body of their own volition, there'll be more to come.
"I expect that these kinds of attacks will keep occurring," he said, adding that they would likely "grow in severity and in frequency".
"I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."
Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.
And a string of other rogue AI incidents have also been made public this year, including a case where a digital assistant - without instruction - booted someone off a pilates class waiting list in a bid to get an Australian man in .
Several AI firm leaders themselves - including Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk - have said the speed at which AI is developing is dangerous to humanity and needs to be reined in.
But the US and China, who are vying for AI supremacy, are roadblocks. Both are hostile to greater regulation, wanting the economic and technological spoils of AI, and have downplayed safety concerns.

REalloys CEO Lipi Sternheim told Fox News Digital that a win would mean keeping rare-earth supplies flowing to defense manufacturers for the next 2-3 years, giving American companies time to build domestic production and reduce China’s leverage.
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for a summit with President Donald Trump, four months after the two leaders reached a sweeping agreement that included Chinese commitments on rare earths, agricultural purchases, trade and investment.
Trump hailed that agreement as a breakthrough for American farmers, manufacturers and workers. But the latest talks come amid uneven progress on commitments involving rare-earth minerals, agricultural and commercial purchases, trade and investment, while key disputes over tariffs, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, intellectual property and Taiwan remain unresolved.
Under the May agreement, China committed to address U.S. concerns over rare-earth supplies and purchase at least $17 billion a year in U.S. agricultural products, while also approving an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft, restoring market access for American beef and resuming poultry imports. The two countries also chartered new boards on trade and investment.
CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE
President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping during a welcome ceremony at the Great Hall of the People, Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Beijing. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo)
Four months later, implementation has been uneven. Reuters reported that China is making progress toward finalizing its commitment to purchase 200 Boeing jets, while agricultural imports are projected to fall short of the agreed level and the new trade and investment boards are still being put into operation.
AI is expected to be a major focus of the two-day summit, along with possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods and discussions over China’s rare-earth exports, according to a senior administration official. The May agreement, when Trump and Xi last met, also chartered new U.S.-China boards on trade and investment, though it did not resolve the broader economic and national security tensions between the two countries.
REalloys CEO Lipi Sternheim told Fox News Digital China’s dominance of the rare-earth supply chain gives Beijing leverage over U.S. defense and technology industries, warning that the Trump-Xi meeting must preserve supplies while American production ramps up.
"The fact that Trump and Xi are meeting and the main topic of the day is rare earths probably tells you and the American people all they need to know about the importance," said Sternheim.
Sternheim said the immediate goal of the Trump-Xi meeting should be to keep rare earths flowing to U.S. defense manufacturers for the next two to three years, giving American companies time to build domestic mining, processing and magnet-making capacity and reduce their dependence on China.
THE WEST STILL DOESN’T GRASP THE DANGER OF CHINA’S RARE EARTH ENDGAME
Chinese President Xi Jinping, left, shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, Thursday, May 14, 2026. (Kenny Holston/Pool Photo via AP)
He said that rare earth minerals are used to make the powerful magnets found in cellphones, electric vehicles, drones, robots and defense systems, including missiles, F-35 fighter jets , submarines and missile-defense systems.
Heavy rare earths are especially important for high-temperature applications such as missiles and space systems, but China controls most of the mining, processing and magnet-making capacity. Sternheim cautioned that shifting production to the U.S. will not happen quickly.
"You can’t build 40 years in two days," Sternheim said, adding that it will take years.
Trump touted the U.S. lead over China in artificial intelligence during an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, while declaring that U.S. government documents would begin referring to the technology as "superintelligence."
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD
President Donald Trump meets with China's President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People, Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Beijing. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo)
"Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," said Trump. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. That's the group that wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way."
While Trump and Xi will be in meetings, first lady Melania Trump is expected to accompany Xi’s wife Peng to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art .
The two will "explore works spanning centuries of artistic achievement and Sino-American cultural exchange."
Thursday will begin with a prestigious State Arrival Ceremony, including 479 military personnel from all branches on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House.
The day will end with a state dinner with high-profile guests, including many from the tech world.
Those guests will include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former senior White House adviser Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook.

articles.title_zh: Bonds shaky, oil eases off highs amid trade, peace talks
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Marc Jones and Rocky Swift
LONDON/TOKYO, Sept 24 (Reuters) - World financial markets remained on edge on Thursday after concerns about the Iran war and inflation pain had triggered the sharpest selloff in US Treasuries and other benchmark government bonds since last year's Liberation Day turmoil.
Bond yields were nudging higher again in Europe as ‌oil prices moved back above $105 a barrel and as traders waited for what could be a tense meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi ‌Jinping in Washington later.
The 10-year US Treasury yield - the benchmark of the $29-trillion Treasury market that anchors pricing for virtually all financial assets globally - touched a new post-financial-crisis high of 5.145% in early European trading.
The difference between what France and ​Germany pay to borrow was also at its widest since Mario Draghi's "Whatever it Takes" speech of 2012, while Japan's 10-year yield had jumped to a 30-year high overnight in Asia.
Strong PMI data and a weak US government bond sale had compounded Wednesday's global rout and AXA's Chief Economist Gilles Moec said all the ingredients were now in place for a rise in long-term interest rates.
"Inflation is high, central bankers are giving hawkish messages, there's competition from the funding needs of the tech sector and there are no reassuring signs on the US debt trajectory," Moec said.
"They are all fairly big macro ‌issues and on top of that you have the binary geopolitical ⁠issue of what is happening in the Middle East."
The latest rise in oil came as doubts grow again about the chance of a US-Iran deal, despite the talks at the UN this week. Reports have also suggested that Trump is considering a possible export ban on US-produced diesel.
Analysts ⁠at Deutsche Bank pointed to Iran foreign ministry comments that it had presented a list of conditions to the US for restarting truce talks, that included the acceptance of a shipping route agreed by Oman and Iran, along with an end to the naval blockade and the release of Iran's frozen assets.
And Iran's President Pezeshkian struck a defiant tone, saying that Iran would not allow freedom of navigation through Hormuz ​while ​the US blockade and sanctions remained in place.
MSCI's main world share index, the pan European STOXX 600 and ​Wall Street futures all moved lower amid the unsettled mood. [.EU]
History offers some ‌guidance on how painful spikes in bond market borrow costs can be for stocks. The MSCI world index halved in value after the last time the 10-year Treasury yield broke 5%, which was just before the global financial crash.
It suffered a similar slump less than a decade earlier too when a near 6.8% spike helped pop the dotcom bubble.
"There is definitely angst in the bond market. There are no two ways about it," said Pictet Asset Management strategist Arun Sai.
"We are going through a period where the steady state equilibrium has been challenged in a number of ways, and it's competing narratives, and it's not yet obvious which of these is right," he added.
Xi and Trump's meeting later is part of Xi's first trip to the US ‌in nearly three years and comes after Trump visited China earlier in the year.
Analysts expected few if any ​major breakthroughs, but the news on Wednesday was that Washington and Beijing could extend their 11-month trade truce.
Treasury Secretary ​Scott Bessent said they had reached a deal on an initial 2-month extension as ​Trump greeted Xi personally at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
In the currency market, the dollar was hovering at a two month high against a basket ‌of other top world currencies following the sharp rise in Treasury yields ​which effectively makes dollar-denominated assets more attractive.
Following Wednesday's ​hot PMI data, traders also now see a nearly 70% chance of another increase when the US Federal Reserve next meets in October, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool, up from 50% a week ago.
On the economic front, the US Labor Department is expected to report later that initial jobless claims likely rose to 201,000 in the week ​ended September 19, while continuing claims likely increased 15,000 to 1.745 ‌million in the prior week. New home sales are forecast to edge up to 615,000 units in August from 607,000 units in July.
Speeches are also due from ​a flock of Fed and ECB officials on Thursday, including New York Fed President John Williams and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and ECB Executive Board ​members Isabel Schnabel and Philip Lane.
(Additional reporting by Naomi Rovnick in London; Editing by Louise Heavens)

articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Oil prices back up as U.S. and Iran trade fresh threats to expand 7-month war
articles.content_orig:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said President Trump's remarks to the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, about deciding whether to "annihilate" Iran, prompted him to alter his own address to the summit.
"With regard to the statements made by the U.S. president, the text of the speech that had been prepared before the trip for presentation at the UN General Assembly was set aside," Pezeshkian told journalists in New York.
He said it prompted him to change the approach to discussing "ourselves, America's behavior and the actions that Israel is carrying out."
Criticizing Mr. Trump's remarks, in which the U.S. president said he had a "big decision" to make about whether to drive Iran "into hell," Pezeshkian said: "They cannot destroy Iran; Iran is a country that has roots in history."
Referring to Iran's diplomatic activity during the visit, he said meetings had been held with officials from several countries, including the Iraqi prime minister and the Swiss president, with "good understandings and areas for cooperation" discussed.
Through a translator, Pezeshkian told the summit Wednesday that Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and that the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."
Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian added.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps posted a video Thursday on its Telegram social media channel purportedly showing the aftermath of its attack the previous day on a cargo vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the description provided by the IRGC, the video "confirms that at least one projectile struck the violating vessel on Wednesday morning."
Oman's navy said Wednesday that it had come to the rescue of the vessel's crew, one of whom was killed in the attack on the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao. Oman said 27 crew members were evacuated from the stricken ship.
The strike on a cargo vessel was first reported earlier Wednesday by the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center.
In its social media post Thursday, the IRGC said the ship was targeted for "transiting the Strait of Hormuz along an unauthorized and unsafe route."
Iran has demanded for weeks that all ships wishing to transit the strait seek permission from its military, rejecting repeated U.S. assertions that a southern route through the vital shipping channel, close to Oman's coast, is safe and available.
Global oil prices jumped Thursday, with international benchmark Brent crude surging 3% percent to hit $106.24 per barrel before easing slightly as uncertainty swirled around the seven-month U.S. war with Iran.
Hopes for a deal to get Gulf oil and gas flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz as global leaders gathered for the United Nations General Assembly in New York had sent oil prices down for about two weeks, until Wednesday.
But as world leaders offered little to suggest any progress toward ending the turmoil that has choked tanker traffic in the Middle East, crude oil prices renewed their ascent.
Benchmark U.S. crude rose about 2% to trade just under $94 a barrel early Thursday, while Brent remained up over 2%, selling at over $105 before markets opened in the U.S.
The price for Brent crude has remained much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel jointly launched their war with Iran. Talks between the U.S. and Iran, via mediators, have resumed this week, but nothing concrete has come from the discussions.
The price rises also come as Iran warns that any renewed U.S. attacks — which President Trump has threatened repeatedly to order this week —   could draw retaliation with expanded targeting of energy infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea and possibly even the Indian Ocean.
Major General Yahya Safavi, a senior military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, warned Thursday that any resumption of hostilities by the United States could see Iran and its allies expand their attacks on global energy supplies in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and possibly even stretch to the Indian Ocean.
"If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait may open before their eyes," warned Safavi, a former commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The Bab el-Mandeb, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, is the Middle East's second major shipping chokepoint, and it has become vital to Saudi energy exports as the ongoing U.S.-Iran war severely impedes traffic in the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz.
"Are they prepared to enter a battle on this front? This is a question they should pay more attention to," Safavi said, asserting that the Houthis had "full control" over the Bab el-Mandeb and access to the Red Sea.
"I think that the connection between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, will change the battlefield," he said, stressing the link between Iran and its Houthi allies as "a shared destiny — both in terms of common interests and common threats."
"The war front could become broader," he said, extending even "to the Indian Ocean or elsewhere."
Already the Houthis have attacked Saudi ships in the Red Sea  and infrastructure and vowed to impose a blockade of the kingdom's Red Sea ports. The group claims it is retaliation for ongoing Saudi military strikes in support of Yemen's government, which has been engaged in a civil war against the Houthis for more than a decade.
There were eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since it began its record-long deployment about 10 months ago, according to a letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that was obtained Wednesday by CBS News.
CNN was first to report on the letter. A Navy official confirmed it was sent Tuesday.
The deployment of the Lincoln and its approximately 5,000 crew members came under scrutiny after family members of the sailors and members of Congress raised questions last month about the conditions aboard the carrier and concerns about the mental health of its service members.
The Lincoln and its strike group were sent to the Middle East after the Iran war broke out. It has since left the region and is returning to its home base of San Diego.
A defense official told CBS News two of the suicide attempts occurred during active fighting with Iran. The letter covers the entire length of the Lincoln strike group's deployment, which began in November of last year.
The strike group includes the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all the embarked aviation squadrons.
The letter was in response to questions from Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York about reported conditions on the ship. In a statement provided to CBS News, Gillibrand said that what President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members."
That the Trump administration "can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable," she added.
The U.S. military blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 115 commercial vessels entering or exiting Iranian ports, according to U.S. Central Command .
The total is an increase of five ships since Monday, when the military last provided an update.
The blockade has become a renewed topic of conflict as Iran and the U.S. renewed negotiations this week at the U.N. General Assembly. Representatives from the United States, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Iranian officials on Tuesday and apparently found some common ground, with President Trump saying the meetings went well.

articles.title_orig: Turkey's Erdogan tells Ukraine's Zelenskiy that Black Sea attacks are inexplicable
articles.title_zh: Turkey's Erdogan tells Ukraine's Zelenskiy that Black Sea attacks are inexplicable
articles.content_orig:
Russia has confirmed diplomatic exchanges over Türkiye’s proposal to halt attacks on ships in the Black Sea , as Ankara seeks to protect grain exports and restore safety for commercial navigation.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Sept. 22 that Türkiye had raised the initiative during recent talks between President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek.
The issue was subsequently pursued through diplomatic correspondence, he said.
Peskov also blamed Ukraine for disruptions to Black Sea grain shipments and said Russia was arranging alternative export routes on Putin’s instructions.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Sept. 19 that Ankara had submitted proposals to both Moscow and Kiev and received responses, although differences remained.
“Frankly, both sides have demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile,” he told broadcaster NTV.
Fidan said securing grain shipments from the Black Sea was Türkiye’s first priority, citing their importance to countries that depend on imports.
A Turkish diplomat told AFP on Sept. 17 that Ankara had shared a draft memorandum with both sides, drawing on the experience of the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative.
The approach would build on Ukraine’s existing shipping route along the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.
Another route could follow the coastlines of Georgia and Türkiye, subject to the participation of the countries concerned.
The aim is to make greater use of coastal states’ territorial waters to reduce vessels’ exposure to attacks.
Separately, the Turkish Agricultural Diplomacy Group has proposed protecting grain terminals, silos, warehouses and loading facilities.
Its plan also calls for a voluntary registry to verify participating vessels’ civilian status, cargoes and routes, with Türkiye serving as a coordination center.
The diplomatic effort follows a rise in attacks on commercial shipping.
At least 25 Turkish-owned vessels had been hit since late June, including four sailing under the Turkish flag.
Fidan said earlier this month that Turkish and Azerbaijani sailors had been killed in attacks, warning of risks to navigation, food supplies and energy trade.
Erdoğan raised the issue with U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in New York on Sept. 22, expressing concern over attacks on commercial vessels and urging all parties to act responsibly to protect Black Sea shipping.
Türkiye and the United Nations brokered the original grain agreement in July 2022.
It enabled the export of nearly 33 million tons of grain and other foodstuffs from Ukrainian ports before Russia withdrew in July 2023.
The U.S.-backed Board of Peace is proposing a six-month, $2.45 billion plan to begin reconstruction and governance in Gaza as President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan struggles to stay afloat.
When Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war, choking off sea passage for some 15 million barrels of oil a day, many feared that prices would skyrocket, cratering the world economy.
Amedspor wrote a new chapter in Turkish football history on Sept. 20 night, defeating Beşiktaş 3-2 at home to claim the Süper Lig summit heading into the three-week international break.

articles.title_orig: Elizabeth Holmes to Transfer to Halfway House in August 2027
articles.title_zh: Elizabeth Holmes to Transfer to Halfway House in August 2027
articles.content_orig:
Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center.
Theranos founder and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has been approved for placement in a community correction center, or halfway house, and is scheduled to be placed there next year, according to an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System, ABC News has learned.
Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027, according to the notification.
When reached for comment on Wednesday, the Federal Bureau of Prisons said in a statement that it "does not discuss the conditions of confinement for any individual, including release plans."
"Additionally, per BOP policy, specific designation information cannot be released until after an individual arrives at their designated institution," the statement continued.
BOP said several factors go into assigning individuals to facilities, including "the level of security and supervision required, medical or programmatic needs, separation or security considerations necessary for the individual’s safety, and other relevant factors, such as proximity to the individual’s release residence."
Holmes was originally sentenced in 2022 to 11 years and 3 months in prison for defrauding investors with false claims about her company's blood-testing technology.
Her sentence has since been reduced to 10 years and 3 months, and she is now scheduled to be released on Feb. 22, 2030. According to the Victim Notification System, upon her release, Holmes will reside in Austin, Texas, and be supervised by the United States Probation Office there.
The new release date was the result of a retroactive change to federal sentencing guidelines and earned time through the First Step Act.
"To be clear, this sentence reduction does not diminish the enormity of Holmes's crimes, nor does it ignore the significant negative impact her conduct has had on the community," U.S. District Judge Edward Davila wrote in a March order granting a motion to reduce her sentence. "The hundreds of millions of dollars in losses caused by Holmes's fraud speak for themselves. And though unquantifiable, the echoes of the immense reputational damage that the innovative industry in Silicon Valley suffered as a consequence of Holmes's deception still reverberate to this day. Holmes's revised sentence continues to reflect a just punishment for her serious offense and serves as a reminder that the scales of justice will balance."
Holmes was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud while at the helm of Theranos. She reported to prison in May 2023.
Last year, a U.S. appeals court upheld the fraud convictions and $452 million restitution order for Holmes and her second-in-command, Ramesh "Sunny" Balwani.
The two had argued the court committed several legal errors and violated their constitutional rights during their separate trials. The three-judge panel for the appeals court rejected their claims, finding that any errors were harmless or that their arguments failed to show any violation.
Holmes is the subject of a forthcoming documentary by filmmaker Nathan Fielder , "You Can See Everything." In a new trailer for the film released Wednesday, Holmes maintained that she "did not" do anything wrong.
She participated in the documentary in 2023, before reporting to prison.

articles.title_orig: Florida governor candidate Byron Donalds stands by Trump after some mentions of the president removed from website
articles.title_zh: Florida governor candidate Byron Donalds stands by Trump after some mentions of the president removed from website
articles.content_orig:
Some prominent references to President Trump were scrubbed from Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds' campaign website in recent weeks — but the Republican said Wednesday he isn't backing away from the president's agenda.
During an onstage interview at the Sunshine Economy Summit, Donalds said his campaign has "been working on website changes for, like, two months now." He said the changes are meant to reinforce the campaign's key policy themes ahead of the general election, including affordability.
"These are the issues we talk about every day on the campaign trail," he told Tom Hudson of public media organization WLRN. "For the general election, the voters of Florida want to know the policies you're going to implement to make their lives better. And so, we wanted to make sure that the website fully reflected the vision and the policies for the future of Florida."
Asked whether the changes suggest that he no longer intends to "enact the Trump agenda," a phrase that his campaign site previously listed as one of its top issues, Donalds said: "No, I think that's a separate question."
Donalds called the president's agenda a "common-sense agenda" that is "centered around law and order, sound markets, making sure that we secure our nation's borders, making sure that we continue to work with the federal government when it comes to immigration policy."
The summit, which was hosted by the Greater Fort Lauderdale Alliance, also featured an interview with Donalds' opponent, Democratic nominee David Jolly.
Previously, Donalds' status as a staunch Trump ally was difficult to miss. The homepage of his campaign website noted several times that Donalds was endorsed by Mr. Trump, and it featured a photo of the president and the congressman giving thumbs-up signs to the camera, according to an archived version of the site from earlier this month. The site's "Issues" page was also topped by a promise to "Enact the Trump Agenda."
Now, Donalds' nod from the president still appears on a scrolling list of endorsements from conservative figures, and his role as a 2024 Trump campaign surrogate is mentioned, but the president's name does not appear as extensively. The "Issues" page also no longer names the president, instead leading with the slogan: "Accountable, Achievable, Affordable!"
The changes, first reported by the Miami Herald on Tuesday, drew nationwide attention and generated speculation about whether Donalds is seeking to keep the president at arm's length.
Donalds has closely aligned himself with the president for years. Ahead of the 2024 race, he endorsed Mr. Trump over Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in the GOP primary.
Mr. Trump endorsed Donalds last year, shortly before he formally launched his campaign .
"Byron Donalds would be a truly Great and Powerful Governor for Florida and, should he decide to run, will have my Complete and Total Endorsement," Mr. Trump said. "RUN, BYRON, RUN!"

articles.title_orig: ‘America’s Got Talent’ Crowns Season 21 Champion
articles.title_zh: ‘America’s Got Talent’ Crowns Season 21 Champion
articles.content_orig:
Dreams do come true. That’s certainly the case for Nene Royal, the precocious talent who was tonight crowned winner of America’s Got Talent .
The 16-year-old Thai singer and guitarist has electrified audiences — and AGT ‘s judges — throughout this 21st season.
When it mattered most, the teen sensation captured the heart of the nation. She won America’s vote and captured the title, announced during the two-hour results show which aired Wednesday night (Sept. 23) on NBC .
As the champion, Royal earns more than bragging rights. She scores the $1 million grand prize and a headlining spot in a live show in Las Vegas.
See latest videos, charts and news
Special guests and performers during the live results show included Josh Groban, Lele Pons, REI AMI, Steve Aoki, and Linkin Park who, following America’s Vote, collaborated with Royal for a performance of “The Emptiness Machine.”
Hailing from Phuket, Thailand, Royal picked up the guitar at age seven and has always dreamed of being a “superstar on tour,” she explained during the auditions phase of AGT . She delivered the goods in a massive way, by belting-out a reinterpreted cover of The Cranberries mid-‘90s protest anthem “Zombie.”
With her spot in the quarterfinals, Royal proved she was no one-hit wonder. Her cover of Soundgarden’s “Black Hole Sun” was such a blast, it earned Mel B’s Golden Buzzer. With that, the youngster advanced to the finals.
For her performance in the season 21 finale, Nene reimagined the White Stripes’ classic 2000s number “Seven Nation Army,” grinding Jack White’s iconic riff into a heavy weapon and introducing a fresh guitar solo. The youngster wore a traditional dress, emblazoned with the words “Nene Thailand.”
“Well, I’m glad I pressed my Golden Buzzer,” Mel B remarked after the amps were turned off. “Because not only do you have such mysterious, mystical stage presence, you’re from the best place in the world, Phuket, Thailand…and what you’re bringing to this competition is so unique and you’re only 16 years old. If you don’t win this, I am going to sell Howie’s new house.”
Sofía Vergara said she was confident that the “world is going crazy because there is nothing like you right now, you are unique.”
Howie Mandel spoke last. Nene, he enthused, is “the biggest, most talented, most viral talent to be on that stage…you should win. Give her the million, America.”
The veteran actor spoke truth. It was a winning performance. For the record, magician Geno Ploeger came in second, and magician group Hundred Fingers completed the podium in third place.

articles.title_orig: ‘Survivor 51’ premiere recap: The Open Era is just the jolt we needed
articles.title_zh: ‘Survivor 51’ premiere recap: The Open Era is just the jolt we needed
articles.content_orig:
After celebrating its 50th season, Survivor has officially entered a new "era" — and host Jeff Probst means that literally.
Survivor 51 premiered Wednesday on CBS with a two-hour episode, sending a new cast of 21 players to Fiji to compete for a prize that starts at $1 million — but could grow to $2 million this season. The cast ranges in age from 24 to 49 and includes a Grey's Anatomy actor, a wrestler, a chef and a federal prosecutor.
The season arrives four months after Survivor 50 , which reunited former contestants from across the franchise and saw Aubry Bracco crowned the winner in May.
What sets the new season apart is the format. Probst has called it the start of the "Open Era" — the show's first major reset since 2021. The premiere offered the first look at what that means. Here's all you need to know.
The Open Era follows the show's New Era, which began with Survivor 41 in 2021. The format shake-up is designed to make the game more unpredictable than ever, according to Probst.
"The Open Era is taking the massive uncertainty [from Survivor 50 ] and making it permanent," he said during the Survivor 50 finale. "The idea is that anything that has ever happened at any time on the show can happen in any season, at any time, in any order — without any warning."
In an interview with TV Insider , Probst said the season represented a "new type of Survivor game." He said, "Imagine a giant treasure chest and inside that chest is every single thing we have ever done in 25 years and 50 seasons of Survivor . The question is, each season, what are we going to pull out and put into the season?"
The twist, in other words, is that there is no telling what the twist is . During the premiere, all 21 contestants started the game together on a single beach. Lewis Kelly volunteered to leave the group and was sent to Exile Island, a twist that has appeared in previous seasons. The remaining contestants were later split into two tribes, Savu and Toka.
Probst also gave the players the chance to vote on whether to eliminate the fire-making challenge, which determines who earns the last spot in the final three. The vote had to be unanimous, but only five players voted to get rid of it, so the challenge will remain this season.
The prize money could grow to $2 million this season.
The Open Era marks another evolution for a show that has repeatedly changed its format. When the New Era began, the game was shortened from 39 to 26 days, and producers moved away from seasons built around specific themes. At the time, Probst told Parade that the aim was to create a "faster, more dangerous and much more intense game."
But the Open Era presents a different challenge, especially for superfans who think they know Survivor inside and out. "The superfan may be at a disadvantage now," Probst told TV Insider, "because the assumptions that really helped you in previous seasons are your enemy now, because it could literally be anything."
After Toka lost the first immunity challenge, the tribe had to vote out one of its members.
The decision came down to Aaliyah Puglia and Jenna Doore, who both tried unsuccessfully to gain safety through the show's Shot in the Dark twist.
Puglia was ultimately voted out 6-2.
The Open Era introduces a twist that could significantly increase the amount of prize money at stake.
The coin flip was introduced in Survivor 50 , when Rick Devens correctly called the toss, earning immunity and adding $1 million to the grand prize. Bracco ultimately won the season and its $2 million prize.
The coin flip will return in Survivor 51 , but with a new rule. If the player wins the flip, an extra $1 million will be added to the $1 million prize. If they lose, the money will roll over to the next season.
That means if the coin flip isn't won this season, a player on Survivor 52 could flip for an extra $2 million, bringing the total prize to $3 million. If they lose too, the money will keep rolling over until someone wins it.
"It will go until it pays off and then it'll start again," Probst told the Hollywood Reporter . He added, "I think it's the most innovative twist in prize money in the history of unscripted television, because that million dollars is a living, breathing thing. And the question is, where is it going to land and how many of them will there be when it does land?"
While Survivor 51 features an entirely new cast, returning players aren't necessarily gone for good in the Open Era.
Probst told Variety in May that another season featuring former contestants could happen, although there were no plans at the time. "There's nothing on the horizon, but they're very fun to do — for us as well," he said. "And now we have enough players, we might be able to pull off something that includes returning players sooner than the period of time we had since the last one. But I don't know. We know what we're doing for 51 and 52. That's it."
Survivor 51 was filmed on Fiji's Mamanuca Islands, which have been the show's home since Season 33.
Speaking at an event in May , Probst said the location was "a logistics issue and not really a creative choice." He added, "Fiji has actually saved Survivor , and our relationship with their government and all the landowners is amazing. If that changed, we'd be back looking desperately for somewhere."

articles.title_orig: Packers Wire staff predictions: Week 3 vs. Falcons
articles.title_zh: Packers Wire staff predictions: Week 3 vs. Falcons
articles.content_orig:
The Green Bay Packers will attempt to win a second consecutive game and get to 2-1 to start 2026 while also extending the team's record home opener win streak to 14 games when the Atlanta Falcons come to Lambeau Field for "Thursday Night Football" in Week 3. Matt LaFleur's team has looked shaky through two weeks, but a chance to come home and play a struggling Falcons team could be just what the doctor ordered.
Here’s how the staff at Packers Wire believes the Week 3 showdown with the Falcons will go down:
On a scale of 1-10, my confidence level in a Packers victory is not high, maybe a 5 or 6. If the Falcons had any kind of pulse, this would feel like a true toss up game given the state of the offensive line, and how so much of what has ailed the Packers is centered on the offensive line's play through two weeks. That said, if there's a more troubled offensive team entering Week 3, it's the Falcons, who are returning their quarterback but still have massive problems. Overall, the Packers defense has been a real strength, so even if Green Bay's offense struggles to sustain drives once again, I think a takeaway or two will probably swing the game in the right direction. Winning ugly might just be the way forward until the rebuilt offensive line settles in. Defense. Special teams. Don't mess it up on offense. That should be the plan for Thursday night.
Green Bay’s offense has looked rough through the first two weeks, and it’s unclear when/if it will get better. Losing Jayden Reed for an unspecified amount of time and Zach Bako-Bewele for the season won’t help. The Packers’ offensive grade from Pro Football Focus is 55.8, tied for last with the Falcons. I’m not expecting a high-scoring affair Thursday night. Michael Penix Jr. is set to make his season debut for the Falcons and could show signs of rust. Atlanta can try feeding Bijan Robinson, but Green Bay’s run defense is eighth in rushing yards allowed per game. The Falcons' defense is first in rushing yards allowed per game, but the Packers haven’t been able to run the ball much anyway. Green Bay has the better quarterback, but the pass-blocking hasn’t given Jordan Love enough time to operate the offense efficiently—he currently has the lowest completion percentage (52.1%) in the league among quarterbacks with at least 30 pass attempts. Atlanta’s pass rush has already generated 48 pressures, but I still like the Packers in their home opener.
The home opener should provide a friendlier environment for Green Bay’s offense to hopefully find some kind of rhythm, but missing Zach Bako-Bewele and Aaron Banks will not help the already worrisome O-line, and the Falcons have been generating pressure at a high rate, even if it has been more of the slow burn variety. Even on a short week and without two starting O-linemen and Jayden Reed, I’m backing them to put up more points this time around, as well as Jonathan Gannon continuing to tweak his defense to hold Michael Penix and the Atlanta offense in check. The Packers need a ‘get right’ game, and Thursday night presents a big opportunity.
The Packers offense needs to get rolling and it starts by getting Tucker Kraft more involved. Atlanta’s defense just gave up two touchdowns to Darren Waller and in week one they gave up a touchdown to Pat Freiermuth. I fully expect the pride of Timber Lake to have a monster game in primetime to remind everyone just how special he is. On the flip side Green Bay’s defense, along with their special teams play is the reason they won last week. They could turn in their best performance of the young season in front of the Lambeau Field crowd. Give me the Packers by double digits.

articles.title_orig: Harrison Jr. blocking out noise amid slow start for Cardinals
articles.title_zh: Harrison Jr. blocking out noise amid slow start for Cardinals
articles.content_orig:
Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. has only caught one pass through two games this season. But he doesn’t think he needs to change anything.
Asked if he’s losing confidence, Harrison said he knows he’s preparing the right way, and that’s all that matters.
“Does your confidence come from results or does your confidence come from your process?” Harrison said, via ESPN. “And I think for me it comes from my process. So, my process isn’t going to change whether I get zero catches or 10 catches. I’m going to still do the same thing week in and week out, Monday through Saturday to prepare myself for games. So, I think that’s where I have a lot of my confidence comes from. And obviously you want to have more of an impact in the game, but I think confidence really has to come from preparation more than anything.”
Harrison said no one player is ever solely responsible for his own production.
“It’s definitely a combination of a lot of things,” Harrison said. “For my route tree getting down the field, you need a lot of things to go right. You need the right coverage, you need protection to hold up, you need me to run a great route, you need obviously Jacoby to make the right pass and make the right read. So, I feel like it’s never one person’s fault for anybody’s success or lack thereof, really. So, I think it’s always a combination of a bunch of things and whether that’s a lack of success or success in general.”
Harrison’s comments may be true, and yet there’s no denying that he has been a disappointment as the fourth overall pick in the 2024 NFL draft. His rookie year was only OK, he declined in his second season, and through two games in Year 3 he has gone into a steeper decline. Harrison’s process may not change, but something has to change.

Hung Cao, acting US navy secretary, answered questions from US senator Kirsten Gillibrand in a letter
Eight US navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group have attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, revealed in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand on Tuesday.
“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote, responding on behalf of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth to Gillibrand’s inquiry about the quality of life aboard the fleet. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.”
CNN first reported on Cao’s response to Gillibrand.
The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war.
In August, two military newspapers reported on sailors’ deteriorating mental health, including multiple attempts to jump overboard. The reports prompted outcry from Democrats, who called for an investigation of the conditions onboard.
In March, one sailor’s attempt to go overboard was thwarted by shipmates, according to Cao. In August, one sailor did go overboard. The individual was rescued and received medical treatment, before being “transferred off-ship for follow-up care”, Cao wrote.
MS Now also reported in August on alarming allegations of mold in the ship’s showers and dwindling supplies of food and soap, among other basic necessities.
The number of entrée options was temporarily reduced from two to one, Cao wrote in his letter, a measure “implemented to optimize endurance and ensure sustained time on station”. He said four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
He acknowledged certain delays in replenishing crew supplies.
As details of low morale trickled out of the Lincoln, Hegseth downplayed the media coverage, saying news outlets “ completely misrepresented ” the situation. “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he told reporters in August.
“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a Wednesday statement to the Guardian. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”
“The Navy and the Navy secretary are very committed to sailor health, wellbeing and morale,” a US navy official told the Guardian on Wednesday.

articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is continuing his metaverse while simultaneously pushing forward on AI agents.
At Meta Connect , the Facebook co-founder revealed on Wednesday the Meta VR Glasses, a smaller and slimmer device compared to the company's older Quest-branded family of VR headsets, and a handheld device called the Muse Charm that works with the company's recently released Muse AI personal agent . He revealed the products while speaking on stage at the annual Connect conference for developers.
Zuckerberg shared few details about what Muse Charm can do, only to say that people will be able to speak to the gadget to interact with their Meta AI agents "without having to unlock a phone or open an app." He didn't say how much it would cost, but said that Meta needs to "finalize laying out the components" and is "planning to have this ready to ship in time for the holidays in December."
"We've packed a lot of technology with this little guy," Zuckerberg said. "So, if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The Meta VR Glasses are slimmer and lighter than the company's older Quest-branded VR headsets, but they are also more expensive, costing $1,299 when they go on sale in spring 2027. They represent Meta's first VR device since 2024, when the company debuted the $299 Quest 3S.
The Meta VR Glasses are powered by an external puck that houses a Qualcomm processor and battery, allowing it to function as a mini-computer that also helps reduce the glasses' overall weight and size. The glasses are able to display better visuals than the older Quest headset, and contain sensors that track users' eyes and hand movements, which reduces the need to use controllers to interact with the device.
"We have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion, high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time," Zuckerberg said.

articles.title_orig: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.title_zh: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.content_orig:
Editorial Director/Box Office Editor
UPDATED: A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount ‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference.
The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood . According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison ‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday.
The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures.
“It feels like a scramble,” one source said.
To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it.
“It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.”
Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed.
Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told.
The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers).
But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that.
“We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery.
Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt.
On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove -like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule.
The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18. To date, the Denis Villeneuve franchise counts $1.12B at the global box office and eight Oscars.
We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution. Warner Bros international distribution has more of a solid presence in offshore territory offices and staffers than Paramount, which needs to untangle itself from UIP. Paramount could find great muscle in Warners International distribution and marketing infrastructure.
While we were told by Paramount sources that the plan isn’t to create two studios, it might be wise for Ellison to keep each respective marketing team at their respective labels if he wants each studio working to the top of their creative merits and box office strengths: former Warner Bros exec Josh Goldstine presiding over global marketing and distribution at Paramount, and the team he built at Warners — Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford–exactly over at Warners. Marketing and distribution rolls up and reports into the motion picture heads. During Warner Bros’ $4.38B grossing 2025, the trio of Nussbaum, Davin, and Stanford achieved great innovative marketing efficiencies, we’re told, and yes, those 11 Oscars for the Burbank, CA lot.
There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff.
Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching.
The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership.
“Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.”
And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal.
What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.”
Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.”
For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground.
Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros.
